name: pinneapple_catalog

children.name: pinneapple_catalog.costs
children.doc:
Measured cost of every method in the catalog (#52, roadmap D1).

``pinneapple_analysis.cost`` answers "how much does this operation cost" for one callable. This module applies it to
the catalog: one probe per method, run here, on this machine, and stored in ``method_costs.json`` next to the
catalog itself. Every number in that file came out of a run, never out of a formula:

- **time**: median of repeated runs at each problem size, with the interquartile range as the spread;
- **memory**: peak increase over the starting footprint, and ``mem_source`` says how it was sampled (``rss`` with
  psutil, ``"tracemalloc"`` without it -- which sees Python and NumPy only);
- **FLOPs**: only where a PyTorch path makes them countable, and ``flops_source`` says whether the count is exact
  (``flop_counter``) or a lower bound (``profiler``); ``null`` is a real answer, not a gap to fill with a guess;
- **scaling exponent**: the log-log slope of cost against problem size, with a bootstrap confidence interval, and
  the verdict against the complexity the probe declares.

The **machine** is recorded with the numbers (CPU, cores, platform, Python and torch versions), because a wall time
without its machine cannot be compared with anything. Two runs on two machines are two different measurements;
:func:`compare_with_baseline` refuses to compare across machines for exactly that reason.

Coverage is a first-class value, not an afterthought: :func:`coverage` returns one row per catalog entry -- every
solver, training method, equation and problem -- and a row is ``measured`` or ``unmeasured`` **with a blocker from the
closed set** :data:`BLOCKERS` (``needs_cuda``, ``needs_external_solver``, ``needs_optional_package``, ``needs_input``,
``not_a_single_operation``, ``definition``) plus the specific reason: an external solver that is not installed, a GPU
kernel, an entry point that needs a case the probe cannot build. A vague motive cannot hide behind the closed set, and
the gaps can be counted. ``scripts/measure_method_costs.py --check`` fails when a catalog method is missing from the
file, when the table has lost the machine its wall times came from, and when an unmeasured row has no blocker or no
reason. ``docs/dev/METHOD_COSTS.md`` is the same table as one line per method, generated by ``--docs`` so it cannot
drift from the numbers.

What a probe measures, exactly: the ``probe`` field names the class or function that ran, and the size axis says what
``n`` means for that method (grid points per side, particles, samples, layers). A family (SPH / ISPH / DFSPH, the
signal decompositions) records which member of the family was timed, so the number is never read as the whole family.

    python scripts/measure_method_costs.py --only S4 S19      # measure a couple of methods, print the table
    python scripts/measure_method_costs.py                    # measure everything with a probe, rewrite the file
    python scripts/measure_method_costs.py --check            # gates: a row per entry, machine recorded, reasons
    python scripts/measure_method_costs.py --docs             # rewrite docs/dev/METHOD_COSTS.md from the table

classes.name: Probe
classes.doc:
One method's measuring stick.

``build(n)`` returns the callable that does the work at problem size ``n`` (its setup is not timed, as in
:func:`pinneapple_analysis.cost.scaling_study`); ``declared`` is the complexity the code claims, so the fitted
exponent has something to be checked against; ``what`` and ``size_axis`` say exactly what was run.

``flops=False`` says the FLOP counter cannot be run on this method in a time that leaves a usable measurement --
it hooks every operator, and an assembly that issues thousands of small ones pays more for the hooks than for the
work. The record then carries ``flops: null`` with an empty source, which is the honest answer and not a gap.

functions.name: machine
functions.doc: What has to travel with a wall time for it to mean anything: the CPU, the cores, the platform, the versions.

functions.name: measure_all
functions.sig: (only: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, repeats: int | None = None, path: Path = COSTS_PATH) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Measure every method that has a probe and write ``path``: the measured records plus the reasons for the rest.

``only`` restricts the run to some ids, leaving the other measured records as they are on disk (so one solver can
be remeasured without touching the others).

functions.name: method_cost
functions.sig: (method_id: str, path: Path = COSTS_PATH) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: One method's record (``measure_all`` does not invent an entry for an id the catalog does not have).

functions.name: coverage
functions.doc:
One row per catalog entry -- every one of them, equations and problems included -- with its status.

``measured`` carries the probe and the fitted exponent; ``unmeasured`` carries the blocker and the reason why no
number was taken; ``missing`` means the table has no row at all (or wrote one without a blocker from
:data:`BLOCKERS` or without a reason), which is a gap in the record rather than a motive, and ``problem`` says
whichever of the two it is.

functions.name: compare_with_baseline
functions.sig: (current: dict[str, Any], baseline: dict[str, Any], *, flops_factor: float = 1.05, time_factor: float = 1.5, mem_factor: float = 1.5) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Regressions between two ``method_costs.json`` documents on the same machine (issue #53's gate).

FLOPs gate tightly (``flops_factor`` 1.05: they are deterministic, so a 6 % rise is a real 6 % rise); time and
memory gate loosely (1.5: the same code on the same machine still moves by tens of percent between runs). A
different machine is refused rather than compared: the same code measured on two CPUs is two measurements, not a
regression.

children.summary: Measured cost of every method in the catalog (#52, roadmap D1).

children.name: pinneapple_catalog.methods
children.doc:
Every solver, training method, equation and problem in PINNeAPPle, with
its code, its references and its validation status.

IDs match the inventory of 2026-09-24 (``docs/dev/PEDIDOS_2026-09-24.md``):
S = solver, T = training method, E = physical equation, P = physical problem.

References come in two kinds, kept apart on purpose:

- ``refs_in_code``: what the module's own docstring already cites.
- ``refs_added``: the canonical source (original paper or standard textbook)
  added here because the code cites nothing. Every arXiv id in both lists
  was checked against the paper title on 2026-09-24 (that check found and
  fixed a wrong id: X-TFC cited arXiv:2005.01219, a metasurface paper, for
  Leake & Mortari; the right id is arXiv:1812.08625).

Validation status (decision D5) is NOT written by hand: it is computed by
``scripts/build_method_status.py`` from ``tests/`` and stored in
``method_status.json``. An item is ``validated`` when a test that exercises
it compares against an independent reference (closed form, published
value or manufactured solution); ``tested`` when tests exist but none is a
reference comparison; ``untested`` otherwise. Anything not ``validated``
is "pending: paper + benchmark" and is left out of ``validated_methods()``.
No code is deleted because of this status.

functions.name: validated_methods
functions.doc: The official list: only items whose last scan found a reference-comparison test.

children.summary: Every solver, training method, equation and problem in PINNeAPPle, with its code, its references and its validation status.

children.name: pinneapple_catalog.resources
children.doc:
Catalog of public Physics AI resources: datasets, CAD/geometry sets,
pretrained models and hosted benchmarks, each with a checked license.

The evaluation behind every entry (what it is, license, size, how we use
it) lives in ``PINNeAPPle-CFD/docs/7.Recursos-publicos.md`` (research of
2026-09-23) plus the PLAID and PressNet checks of 2026-09-24. This module
turns that document into something code can query and enforce: a
component that wants a resource asks the catalog first, and the same
license gate as ``pinneapple_neural._licencas`` refuses non-commercial or
unlicensed resources when ``PINNEAPPLE_COMMERCIAL_MODE=1``.

Rules, matching the research doc:

- ``commercial`` is ``"yes"`` only when the license was read and allows
  commercial use. ``"no"`` is an explicit non-commercial / non-production
  license. ``"unverified"`` covers everything else (no license file, data
  license not declared, conflicting tags) and is treated like ``"no"``:
  a missing license means all rights reserved.
- ``paper`` is filled only with a reference whose arXiv id / DOI was
  checked against the title. Unknown stays ``None``; nothing is invented.
- ``rating`` reuses the doc's classification: ``use_now``, ``product``
  (product level, after the pilot), ``reference`` (reference / internal
  benchmark only) and ``skip`` (outside the CFD scope).

functions.name: list_resources
functions.sig: (kind: str | None = None, domain: str | None = None, rating: str | None = None, commercial_only: bool = False) -> list[Resource]

functions.name: require_allowed
functions.doc: License gate: warns for research-only resources, refuses them in commercial mode.

functions.name: fetch
functions.sig: (resource_id: str, *, allow_patterns = None, local_dir: str | None = None, token: str | None = None, revision: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Download a Hugging Face-hosted resource (after the license gate); returns the local path.

Use ``allow_patterns`` to fetch a subset: several datasets here are terabytes.

children.summary: Catalog of public Physics AI resources: datasets, CAD/geometry sets, pretrained models and hosted benchmarks, each with a checked license.

children.name: pinneapple_catalog.stages
children.doc:
The open tools and the public datasets available at each stage of the physics-AI workflow.

This module answers one question per stage — *what can I use here, and how far does this repository already go?* — for
the thirteen sections the Flow palette is built from (:mod:`pinneapple_flow.palette`, whose ``SECTION_IDS`` a test
compares against :data:`STAGE_IDS`, so the two cannot drift apart silently).

Three catalogues already existed and none of them knew about stages:

* ``pinneapple_data.datasets.catalog`` — the *data*: which public dataset exists, in what format, under what licence,
  and whether there is a reader here. Each entry now carries the stages it feeds (``CatalogEntry.stages``).
* ``pinneapple_analysis.verification.tool_recommendation.TOOL_CATALOG`` — the *solvers*, ranked against a
  ``ProblemSpec``. It says so in its own docstring: it has no ``ML/surrogate`` entries, and its scope is "does this
  tool's documentation cover this PDE", not "what stage of the workflow does it serve".
* ``pinneapple_catalog.resources`` — the *licence gate* over datasets, geometry, models and benchmarks.

Neither of the last two carried a stage, and the libraries that make physics-AI work possible at all (neural operator
packages, ROM toolkits, UQ samplers, optimisers, serving runtimes) were catalogued nowhere. This module is that
missing layer, and it stays a *pointer* table: it does not re-describe a tool whose documented scope already lives in
``TOOL_CATALOG`` — an entry that overlaps says ``also_in`` and the test checks that the id is really there.

What every entry states, and what it refuses to state
-----------------------------------------------------
``license`` is an SPDX id (or the licence's own name where there is no id) read from the artefact that governs the
**code** — the repository's ``LICENSE`` file through the GitHub licence API, or the distribution metadata for a
package that ships none. ``license_verified`` is ``True`` only where that read happened; the entries marked ``False``
are the ones whose licence is stated in a place this checkout did not open, and they say so in ``license_source``.
A verified licence is not a commercial clearance — GPL-3.0 and AGPL-3.0 are read correctly and are still unusable in
a closed product, which is why the id is carried rather than a boolean.

``integration`` is one of three, and only one of them is a claim about this repository:

``"wired"``
    a code path here calls it. ``surface`` then names the module, and a test resolves that module's spec, so an
    entry cannot claim wiring to a file that does not exist.
``"named"``
    the repository mentions it — a recommender, a lazy export, a docstring — without a path that would run it.
``"candidate"``
    nothing here touches it. Most of the map is this, on purpose: the point of the map is to show the distance.

The datasets side is projected from the catalogue rather than copied: :func:`datasets` filters
``pinneapple_data.datasets.catalog`` by stage, so a dataset is catalogued once and tagged, and
:func:`unassigned_datasets` names any catalogued dataset that no stage claims — the entry that would otherwise be
invisible from a stage's point of view.

    >>> from pinneapple_catalog import stages
    >>> [s.id for s in stages.stages()][:4]
    ['problem', 'equations', 'solvers', 'physics_ai']
    >>> [t.name for t in stages.tools(stage_id="physics_ai", integration="wired")][:3]
    ['PyTorch Geometric', 'PhysicsNeMo', 'PySINDy']
    >>> stages.coverage("solvers")["wired"] >= 3
    True

classes.name: Stage
classes.doc:
One step of the workflow: the question it answers, what is here, and the gap that is left.

``kind`` separates the workflow from the palette's last section: ``library`` is the palette's drawer of generated
``auto.*`` calls, not a step of the workflow, so it carries no tools and no question.

classes.name: Tool
classes.doc: One open tool, the stages it serves, and how far this repository already goes with it.

methods.name: is_open
methods.doc:
Whether the licence is an open-source one, by the id's own family (a custom licence that forbids
commercial use is not, however source-available it is).

classes.name: StageTools
classes.doc: One stage of the map: what the outside world offers here, and what this repository already reaches.

methods.name: unverified
methods.doc: Tools whose licence this checkout did not read — the entries a delivery decision cannot rely on yet.

functions.name: tools
functions.sig: (*, stage_id: str | None = None, integration: str | None = None, kind: str | None = None) -> list[Tool]
functions.doc:
The catalogued tools, filtered; sorted by name inside the stage order they serve.

``integration="wired"`` is the list of what this repository actually calls, which is the number that makes the
rest of the map meaningful: everything else is a decision still open.

functions.name: datasets
functions.doc:
The public datasets that feed a stage, projected from ``pinneapple_data.datasets.catalog``.

A dataset is catalogued once and tagged with the stages it feeds (``CatalogEntry.stages``), so this is a filter
over that catalogue rather than a second copy of it. Returns ``[]`` when the dataset catalogue is not importable
(a partial install): the tool map is still useful without it, and the API reports the missing half separately.

functions.name: unassigned_datasets
functions.doc: Catalogued datasets that no stage claims — invisible from a stage's point of view, so named here.

functions.name: coverage
functions.doc:
How far each stage is covered: tools here, tools wired here, and the datasets that feed it.

With ``stage_id=`` it returns that stage's counts; without it, the totals plus the per-stage counts, which is
what a reviewer reads before deciding where the next integration should go.

functions.name: to_json
functions.doc:
The map as JSON-ready dicts — the payload the Engineering API serves.

With ``stage_id=`` one stage; without it, every stage in workflow order plus the totals, so a reader can see
which step is the thin one without calling thirteen times.

children.summary: The open tools and the public datasets available at each stage of the physics-AI workflow.

doc:
Catalog of what PINNeAPPle knows about, with sources.

- ``resources``: public datasets, CAD/geometry sets, pretrained models and
  hosted benchmarks, each with a checked license and a license gate.
- ``methods``: every solver, training method, equation and problem in the
  library, with its code location, its references and its validation status.
- ``stages``: the same question asked the other way round — at each step of
  the physics-AI workflow, which *open tools* exist and which public
  *datasets* feed it, with the licence read and the wiring checked.
summary: Catalog of what PINNeAPPle knows about, with sources.
